scenario: AITA For telling not being friends with women | So I (31M) work in an office and me and this girl (26F) sit at at the same table and talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently she has started asking me to go out for drinks on Friday after work (as friends not a date). I made excuses why I could not for a couple of weeks, but then she asked me if I disliked her, I thought I would just tell her the truth that I do not do friendships with women. I do not recall what I said verbatim however the gist of it is that, if I spend prolonged time with a woman I start feeling for a lack of a better word 'territorial'. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them I my intestines start roiling and I feel an extreme sense of agitation (I never act on it and I put on a happy face and persevere) however I hate said feeling and prefer to avoid it and hence I do not do friendships with women. She then said I should see a psychologist (I will not, even though I am flawed, my flaws make up a part of who I am and I do not wish to change), and since then for the past couple of weeks our talking has just been work related. I thought it would be best to be honest however I am thinking maybe I should have made up some excuse. AITA? Addendum I do get same feelings at work however I do not think about work at home and its work so I have no choice but to tolerate them. However I do not wish to put myself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. I do not wish to feel this way, I know it is not correct, again I never act on it, but I can not help feeling it. I had told this story to a guy I know and he said I must have been be controlling with my previous girlfriends. So just in case people here will make that assumption, it could not be further from the truth. If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys, I think because I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it.

There's a man, let's call him John, who works in an office. He sits at the same table as a woman, let's say her name is Sarah. They talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently, Sarah has started asking John to go out for drinks on Fridays after work, as friends, not as a date. John made excuses for a couple of weeks, but then Sarah asked him if he disliked her. John decided to be honest and told her that he doesn't do friendships with women. He explained that if he spends prolonged time with a woman, he starts feeling territorial. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them, his intestines start roiling, and he feels an extreme sense of agitation. He never acts on it and puts on a happy face and perseveres, but he hates these feelings and prefers to avoid them, hence he doesn't do friendships with women. Sarah then told him he should see a psychologist, which he's not willing to do, even though he knows he's flawed, his flaws make up part of who he is, and he doesn't want to change. Since then, for the past couple of weeks, their talking has just been work-related. John thought it would be best to be honest, but now he's thinking maybe he should have made up some excuse instead. John also mentions that he gets the same feelings at work but doesn't think about work at home and it's work, so he has no choice but to tolerate them. However, he doesn't want to put himself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. He knows it's not correct, but he can't help feeling this way. He told this story to a guy he knows, and the guy said he must have been controlling with his previous girlfriends. John clarifies that it's not true; if the lady is already his, he doesn't mind her talking to or being around other guys because he knows she's his, which makes him happy thinking other men might want what he has and can't have it. So, the question is: Is John's action of being honest with Sarah about not wanting to be friends with women morally acceptable? First, I need to understand the key points here. John feels territorial and agitated when women he's spending time with get attention from other guys. He doesn't act on these feelings but finds them uncomfortable. He chooses not to have friendships with women to avoid these feelings. When Sarah asked him out, he was honest about his feelings, which led to a breakdown in their relationship beyond work. Now, is this action morally acceptable? To determine that, I need to consider the moral principles involved. Some possible principles to consider are honesty, respect for others, autonomy, and the impact of one's actions on others. Honesty is generally considered a moral virtue. Being truthful is important in maintaining trust in relationships. However, honesty can sometimes be hurtful or cause unintended consequences. In this case, John was honest about his feelings, which led to Sarah feeling hurt and their relationship becoming more distant. Respect for others is another important principle. Treating others with dignity and considering their feelings is a key aspect of morality. John's honesty might be seen as respectful because he's being upfront about his boundaries. However, it could also be seen as disrespectful if his honesty is causing unnecessary harm or if his reasons for not wanting to be friends are based on problematic beliefs or feelings. Autonomy refers to the right of individuals to make their own choices. John is exercising his autonomy by choosing not to have friendships with women to avoid discomfort. However, he's also impacting Sarah's autonomy by potentially limiting her social interactions at work. The impact of one's actions on others is crucial. John's honesty led to a change in his relationship with Sarah, making their interactions more formal and work-related. This could be seen as a negative impact on Sarah's social well-being at work, especially if she was looking forward to building a friendship. Another angle to consider is whether John's feelings are based on rational or irrational beliefs. His territorial feelings and agitation when women get attention from others seem to stem from insecurity or possessiveness. These feelings might not be rational and could be indicative of deeper issues, such as jealousy or an insecure sense of self. Furthermore, John's clarification that if the woman is already his, he doesn't mind her interacting with others, suggests that his feelings are more about ownership or control when the woman is not in a committed relationship with him. This could imply that his territorial feelings are more about potential competition rather than genuine concern for the woman's well-being. Considering all these points, John's decision to be honest about not wanting to be friends with women could be seen as both respectful and honest but also potentially hurtful and based on problematic feelings. The moral acceptability might depend on the balance between these factors. On one hand, honesty is important, and John is being upfront about his boundaries. On the other hand, his reasons for not wanting to be friends are based on feelings that could be seen as controlling or possessive, which are not morally commendable. Additionally, his honesty led to a negative impact on Sarah's social well-being at work. Therefore, while honesty is a virtue, the context and the underlying reasons for John's decision make the action morally questionable. His feelings seem to stem from insecurity and possessiveness, which are not healthy or respectful ways to approach relationships. By being honest about these feelings, he might be causing unnecessary harm to Sarah and limiting her autonomy. In conclusion, while the action of being honest is generally morally acceptable, the content of the honesty and the underlying motivations make the action morally unacceptable in this context.
